content: When developing food patterns to reflect real-world settings, we did not use optimization techniques. Instead of relying on serving sizes among consumers, we calculated parameters (percent of energy from food groups and subgroups) based on population-level estimates. This approach included data from both consumers and non-consumers, incorporating zeros into the averaging process. Consequently, the resulting food patterns highlighted nutrient gaps but included quantities smaller than what would typically be consumed by the population consuming the given subgroup. To address nutrient gaps, fortified products were added to the food patterns. For all three fortified items, their impacts were calculated assuming daily consumption. Micronutrient powders (MNPs) do not provide energy, so they did not displace other foods. Instead, the nutrients provided by daily MNPs were added to the food patterns, assuming no changes in child feeding practices. At fixed energy intake levels, both small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) and Super Cereal Plus displaced other food subgroups isocalorically. For SQ-LNS, 20 grams (one sachet) providing 118 kilocalories were included. For Super Cereal Plus, parameters were adjusted based on energy requirements for different scenarios, such as those in Mexico, Bangladesh, and Malawi. The displacement of food subgroups was carefully considered. Super Cereal Plus was treated as a staple food, so staple foods were displaced first, followed by unhealthy items and other food groups. Grains, the most commonly consumed staple food, were displaced first, while milk was displaced last, as beverages were considered less likely to be replaced. However, sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) were displaced earlier, along with other unhealthy items. SQ-LNS, lacking a natural food group home, was often promoted for enriching porridges. It was assumed that younger infants might struggle to consume SQ-LNS on its own, so staple foods were displaced last in this case. The order of displacement for other food groups was the same as for Super Cereal Plus. Nutrient gaps were analyzed by comparing the nutrient content of modeled food patterns to nutrient reference values (NRVs). Gaps were identified for both target and non-target nutrients. For example, gaps for carbohydrates and vitamin D were observed across most groups, even though these were not target nutrients in the modeling. All other NRVs were met for middle and high energy levels across all age/feeding groups. Sensitivity analyses were conducted with revised NRVs, assuming lower iron absorption (5% instead of 10%). When flesh foods were excluded, iron gaps widened, and new gaps for nutrients like thiamin, vitamin B12, copper, magnesium, potassium, and zinc emerged. Eliminating whole grains, vegetables, or various flesh foods introduced multiple new gaps. Scenarios with limited staple food variety or increased staple food quantities were also explored. For infants and children in middle energy intake groups, monotonous staple food patterns resulted in additional gaps for minerals like calcium, magnesium, potassium, and zinc, particularly for the youngest age group. Increasing the minimum quantity of staple foods widened the iron gap but did not introduce other significant micronutrient gaps. The inclusion of unhealthy items, such as biscuits or sugar-sweetened beverages, was modeled to assess their impact on nutrient gaps. For younger infants, even small amounts of these items introduced new gaps for calcium, zinc, and magnesium. Larger quantities of unhealthy items, such as seven servings of biscuits per week, introduced additional gaps for minerals, B vitamins, and choline. Fortified items were evaluated for their ability to address nutrient gaps. Daily MNPs effectively filled the iron gap and substantially reduced the gap for vitamin D. SQ-LNS also reduced the iron gap but introduced a fiber gap when included daily. Super Cereal Plus had limited impact on reducing the iron gap. All fortified items significantly reduced gaps for vitamin D. For breastfed children, daily MNPs filled the iron gap, while SQ-LNS reduced it substantially. However, Super Cereal Plus only slightly decreased the gap without fully addressing it.
